content:
Hi everyone,

I'm a graduate Maths student at Bonn and direct a science nonprofit. We're running a Directed Reading Programme this summer training ~20 strong graduate/advanced-undergrad mathematicians in Lean from scratch. I'd appreciate any feedback on this as I was recommended to put this question here rather than asking personally. The project supervised by Prof. Yang-Hui He from the Maths/ML+AI side. The goal is to train talented human formalisers and bring them to the point where they can contribute real proofs at graduate level — and not just functional formalisers.

We're following the Buzzard/Mehta pedagogical approach (Natural Number Game → MiL → domain-specific Mathlib API → project work), and in weeks 5–7 students work in domain teams on actual Mathlib gaps. Our hard constraint: no new definitions — students formalise proofs using existing Mathlib types and structures only, so we avoid infrastructure work and maximise proof output.

We've done a preliminary audit and identified five candidate project areas. I'd hugely appreciate feedback on:

  1. Are these actually gaps? (Some may exist and we missed them)
  2. Are the prerequisite APIs stable enough for students who are competent but not Mathlib veterans?
  3. Are there better-suited areas we haven't considered — specifically things that are mathematically well-known, clearly missing from Mathlib, and don't require definitional work?

Our candidates:
A. Convergence tests for series (Raabe's test, Kummer's test, Dirichlet's test, Abel's test, Cauchy condensation, Cesàro means, Mertens' theorem on products of series). Using HasSum/Summable/tsum API.
B. Applications of Sylow theory (groups of order p², pq, p²q; classification of groups of small order; "every group of order < 60 is solvable"). Using Sylow/Subgroup/MulAction API.
C. Compactness results in metric spaces (Lebesgue number lemma, Dini's theorem, total boundedness + completeness ↔ compactness, Heine-Cantor). Using MetricSpace/IsCompact/TotallyBounded API.
D. Polynomial irreducibility criteria (Eisenstein, Perron, Schönemann, applications of Gauss's lemma). Using Polynomial/Irreducible API.
E. Finite combinatorics (handshaking lemma, Sperner's theorem, inclusion-exclusion applications, derangement formula, Vandermonde identity). Using Finset/SimpleGraph/Nat.choose API.

A few specific questions:

  • For (A): What's the current status of Mertens' theorem and Cesàro summation? Is the HasSum API comfortable enough for students to work with on convergence tests, or are there known pain points?
  • For (B): Does Sylow.lean expose enough API to state and prove things like "groups of order pq are cyclic when p ∤ q-1," or would students hit infrastructure walls?
  • For (C): How much of the compact ↔ sequentially compact ↔ totally bounded + complete triangle is already done in Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace?
  • For (D): Is Eisenstein's criterion in Mathlib? Gauss's lemma?
  • For (E): Is SimpleGraph.degree developed enough for the handshaking lemma?

Happy to share more details about the programme structure.
Thanks for any pointers!

Raj
(P.S I also put this on Lean for teaching as I wasn't sure where it would be best fit)

We have a lot of materials you mentioned in (C), but you can't find them in Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace simply because most of them are not only true in metric spaces. For example, here's a version of Dini's theorem Monotone.tendstoUniformlyOn_of_forall_tendsto for lattices and a version of Heine-Cantor theorem IsCompact.uniformContinuousOn_of_continuous for uniform spaces. The triangle you mentioned for compactness can be found in Mathlib.Topology.Sequences and Mathlib.Topology.UniformSpace.Cauchy.

For part a, we have NNReal.summable_condensed_iff for Cauchy condensation, Filter.Tendsto.cesaro_smul for Cesaro means, and hasSum_sum_range_mul_of_summable_norm for convergence of the Cauchy product of series. I think indeed we don't have a lot of convergence test for series, so potentially this can be a good project. You can use https://leansearch.net/, https://loogle.lean-lang.org/, or #Is there code for X? to try to find theorems that you mentioned.

(We strongly discourage double-posting here so I removed the other post)

B looks good and I've seen people working on this stuff in the past. It might be challenging in an interesting way to prove that all groups of order less than 60 are solvable. For D surely we have Eisenstein (https://leandex.projectnumina.ai/ points me to https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/RingTheory/Polynomial/Eisenstein/Criterion.html#Polynomial.irreducible_of_eisenstein_criterion).

My instinct is that "try to find gaps in mathlib which are suitable for beginners to fill without having to write any new definitions" is quite a high bar. At Imperial we just encourge people to formalize mathematics which they understand, when we're teaching them.

If you want a fun project related to FLT which is probably very do-able, then you could develop the theory of compact Hausdorff local (commutative) rings. As far as I know this isn't in mathlib, although one nontrivial fact about compact Hausdorff rings (namely, that they're projective limits of finite rings) is being PRed IIUC. See pages 10-15 of https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT/blob/main/2026_EPSRC_TCC_course/20260205.pdf for examples of things I need.
I think all of (E) is in mathlib? At least depending on the form you want, try keyword searching on leansearch.net

Thank you — this is exactly what we needed. The generalisation point is well taken and honestly embarrassing in retrospect: of course Mathlib proves Dini for lattices, not just ℝ. We'll teach our students this lesson early (Week 2 covers Mathlib navigation, and "the result exists but in more generality than you searched for" is clearly a key failure mode to demonstrate).

For Project C, it sounds like the metric-space framing was the wrong cut. We'll either drop it or look specifically for results where the metric structure is essential, not just convenient. Happy to hear suggestions if anything comes to mind.

For Project A, very helpful to know what exists. We'll focus on the convergence tests that seem genuinely absent — Raabe, Kummer, Dirichlet, Abel — and use Loogle/LeanSearch more systematically to verify before committing. Is the HasSum/Summable API reasonably stable for students to build on, or are there known pain points we should prepare them for?

Yongxi Lin (Aaron) said:

We have a lot of materials you mentioned in (C), but you can't find them in Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace simply because most of them are not only true in metric spaces. For example, here's a version of Dini's theorem Monotone.tendstoUniformlyOn_of_forall_tendsto for lattices and a version of Heine-Cantor theorem IsCompact.uniformContinuousOn_of_continuous for uniform spaces. The triangle you mentioned for compactness can be found in Mathlib.Topology.Sequences and Mathlib.Topology.UniformSpace.Cauchy.
HasSum / Summable has existed since forever and hopefully the API is great by now!

Thank you — I've gone through the lecture notes briefly for now and will go through in detail in the coming days. The coefficient ring results (units closed, maximal ideal open/clopen, residue field finite, units topology = subspace topology) look like a well-scoped project for a student team. The proofs are clean point-set topology + basic commutative algebra.

Two questions:

  1. You mentioned the "compact Hausdorff rings are projective limits of finite rings" result is being PRed. Who's working on that? We'd want to coordinate so we're building on top of it rather than duplicating.

  2. For the proof that units are closed (the R × R embedding trick) — is Mathlib's current Units topology set up via this embedding, or would there be API friction?

To be clear about scope: we'd aim at the basic properties of coefficient rings (your pages 10–15), not the Galois representation / ramification / Hopf algebra material further on. That's well beyond what our students can do in 3 weeks

See pages 10-15 of https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT/blob/main/2026_EPSRC_TCC_course/20260205.pdf for examples of things I need.

Sums: the things which beginners find complicated are (a) real-valued sums which are not absolutely convergent are 0 (e.g. 1-1/2+1/3-1/4+...=0 in mathlib, as is 1+2+3+4+...) (b) switching between Real, NNReal and ENNReal (once you've used sums for a while you realise that ENNReal is a fabulous place to do sums because everything converges to the right answer, but then you have to fight your way back to Real sometimes).

The topology on Units is the right topology. Yeah I was just suggesting making API for compact Hausdorff local rings (and I would be open to merging it in FLT; I'm going to need it soon anyway). @Thomas Browning was the person thinking about the deeper result that a compact Hausdorff ring is profinite.

All I've done in this direction is the proof that compact Hausdorff rings are totally disconnected assuming existence of characters on compact Hausdorff abelian groups (which I'm planning to work on in the near future): https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/compare/master...tb65536:mathlib4:tb_chauus
